lead: Water heated at constant pressure passes through three stages: liquid warms to saturation, liquid boils at fixed temperature, and steam superheats. The heat taken in each stage has a name and a symbol. Dryness fraction x tells how much of a wet mixture is vapour, so one number fixes enthalpy, volume and entropy between saturated liquid and saturated vapour. Boiler operators, turbine designers and examiners use these ideas to price steam, check coal use and avoid blade erosion.
prereq: You need: phase names and the p-v-T surface from 5.1, and enthalpy h = u + pv from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Heat 1 kg of water at 20 °C and 1 atm. The temperature rises to 100 °C. The heat added here is sensible heat, because it changes temperature. At 100 °C the water is a saturated liquid: liquid at its boiling point for that pressure. Its specific enthalpy is h<sub>f</sub> = 419 kJ/kg. Specific enthalpy h = u + pv (kJ/kg) counts internal energy and flow work.

More heat at 1 atm does not raise the temperature. Water boils into vapour at 100 °C. This hidden heat is the latent heat of vaporisation h<sub>fg</sub>. At 1 atm h<sub>fg</sub> = 2257 kJ/kg. The energy breaks liquid bonds; it does not raise molecular kinetic energy, so the thermometer stays at 100 °C. When the last liquid disappears, the state is saturated vapour, with h<sub>g</sub> = 2676 kJ/kg. Further heat gives superheated steam: steam above its saturation temperature. At 150 °C the enthalpy is about 2776 kJ/kg.

blocks.where: h<sub>f</sub> is the specific enthalpy of saturated liquid (kJ/kg); h<sub>g</sub> is the specific enthalpy of saturated vapour (kJ/kg); h<sub>fg</sub> is the latent heat of vaporisation (kJ/kg). At 1 atm, 2257 = 2676 − 419.

blocks.text: A boiler burns coal or gas to supply these three buckets of heat. The liquid stage and the superheat stage change temperature. The boiling stage does not.
Wet steam is saturated liquid and saturated vapour together. Dryness fraction x is the mass fraction that is vapour. Some syllabi call x quality; a percentage must be divided by 100 before use.

blocks.where: m<sub>g</sub> is the mass of vapour (kg); m<sub>f</sub> is the mass of liquid (kg); x is the dryness fraction, no unit. x = 0 is saturated liquid; x = 1 is saturated vapour; 0 < x < 1 is wet steam.

blocks.text: Take 1 kg of wet steam. It contains x kg vapour and (1 − x) kg liquid. The liquid part carries h<sub>f</sub> per kg. The vapour part carries h<sub>fg</sub> above h<sub>f</sub> per kg. So the mixture enthalpy is a straight-line rule between the two saturation values.

blocks.where: h is the specific enthalpy of wet steam (kJ/kg); x is dryness fraction; h<sub>f</sub> and h<sub>fg</sub> are taken at the same pressure. For m kg, total enthalpy H = m h (kJ).

blocks.text: Specific volume v and specific entropy s follow the same linear rule, because each is a mass-weighted property in the wet region.
v = v<sub>f</sub> + x (v<sub>g</sub> − v<sub>f</sub>)   and   s = s<sub>f</sub> + x (s<sub>g</sub> − s<sub>f</sub>)
blocks.where: v is specific volume (m³/kg); s is specific entropy (kJ/(kg·K)); subscript f means saturated liquid; subscript g means saturated vapour.

blocks.text: At 10 bar the latent heat 2015 kJ/kg is smaller than 2257 kJ/kg at 1 atm. Higher pressure pushes the liquid and vapour states closer.

A T-v sketch shows a saturation dome. Under the dome is wet steam. A constant-pressure line is horizontal while boiling, and v jumps from v<sub>f</sub> to v<sub>g</sub> as x rises. A T-h sketch has a sloped liquid line, a flat boiling line of length h<sub>fg</sub>, and a sloped superheat line. The flat line is short at high pressure and disappears at the critical point.

The critical point is about 22.1 MPa and 374 °C for water; see 5.2. There hfg = 0, so there is no latent heat and no flat boiling line. Liquid and vapour have the same density. Below the critical point, hfg falls as pressure rises: 2257 kJ/kg at 1 atm, 2015 kJ/kg at 10 bar, zero at critical.

An h-s sketch is the Mollier diagram. In the wet region, lines of constant x lie under the saturation curve. Reading the chart is a skill for 5.4. A throttling calorimeter finds x from a measured temperature, as 5.5 shows. Keep cycle analysis for Unit 6.

figure.caption: At 1 atm, water heats from 20 °C to 100 °C, boils at constant temperature from 419 to 2676 kJ/kg, then superheats. The flat part is the latent heat h_fg = 2257 kJ/kg.

spec.aria: A temperature-enthalpy plot at 1 atm rises from 20 to 100 degrees Celsius, stays flat during boiling from 419 to 2676 kilojoules per kilogram, then rises again in superheated steam.

examples.question: 2 kg of wet steam at 1 atm has dryness fraction 0.9. At 1 atm h_f = 419 kJ/kg and h_fg = 2257 kJ/kg. Find the specific enthalpy h, the total enthalpy H, and the masses of liquid and vapour.
steps: Write the data: m = 2 kg, x = 0.9, h_f = 419 kJ/kg, h_fg = 2257 kJ/kg.
Use the wet-steam rule: h = h_f + x h_fg = 419 + 0.9 × 2257.
The latent part is 0.9 × 2257 = 2031.3 kJ/kg. So h = 419 + 2031.3 = 2450.3 kJ/kg.
Total enthalpy: H = m h = 2 × 2450.3 = 4900.6 kJ.
Mass of vapour: m_g = x m = 0.9 × 2 = 1.8 kg.
Mass of liquid: m_f = m − m_g = 2 − 1.8 = 0.2 kg. Check: (1 − x)m = 0.1 × 2 = 0.2 kg.
examples.answer: The specific enthalpy is 2450.3 kJ/kg, the total enthalpy is 4900.6 kJ, and the mixture contains 1.8 kg vapour and 0.2 kg liquid.
examples.check:
m = 2.0
x = 0.9
hf = 419.0
hfg = 2257.0
h = hf + x * hfg
H = m * h
mg = x * m
mf = m - mg
print(round(h, 1))
print(round(H, 1))
print(round(mg, 1))
print(round(mf, 1))

traps: Using h_fg without multiplying by x: for x = 0.9 the latent part is 0.9 × 2257 = 2031.3 kJ/kg, not 2257 kJ/kg.
Reading 90% quality as x = 90. Divide by 100 first, so x = 0.90.
Using h = x h_g in the wet region. h_g already contains h_f; the correct rule is h = h_f + x h_fg.
Mixing specific and total quantities: h is kJ/kg, H = m h is kJ. A 2 kg sample multiplies by 2.
Using h_f + x h_fg for superheated steam. Superheated steam needs the steam-table value at its pressure and temperature.

quiz.q: Define dryness fraction. State its range and the meaning of x = 0 and x = 1.
quiz.a: x = m_g/(m_f + m_g). Range 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. x = 0 is saturated liquid; x = 1 is saturated vapour.

quiz.q: Why does the temperature not rise while water boils at 1 atm?
quiz.a: At fixed pressure the phase change occurs at the saturation temperature. The heat supplied becomes latent heat, breaking liquid bonds, so it does not raise temperature until all liquid becomes vapour.

quiz.q: Wet steam at 1 atm has x = 0.85, h_f = 419 kJ/kg and h_fg = 2257 kJ/kg. Find h.
5 kg of wet steam at 10 bar has x = 0.92. Take h_f = 763 kJ/kg and h_fg = 2015 kJ/kg. Find the total enthalpy H.
At the critical point h_fg = 0. What does this mean for boiling and for the flat part of a T-h sketch?
quiz.a: There is no latent heat. Liquid changes continuously to vapour without a constant-temperature boiling stage, so the flat line shrinks to a point and h_f = h_g.

quiz.q: A wet steam sample has x = 1. Is liquid present? What is m_f? How does h compare with h_g?
quiz.a: No liquid is present. m_f = 0. The state is saturated vapour, so h = h_g.

quiz.q: Why is h = h_f + x h_fg correct instead of h = x h_g for wet steam?
quiz.a: The liquid part still carries h_f per kg. The vapour part adds h_fg per kg above h_f. The form x h_g ignores the liquid enthalpy and gives a wrong value when x < 1.

beyond: Not for the exam. In power plants, steam leaves a boiler slightly wet, and droplets can erode turbine blades, so operators measure dryness and often add superheat. Above the critical pressure a boiler has no boiling flat part, and the plant is called supercritical. Search for steam dryness fraction, turbine erosion, and IAPWS-IF97 steam properties for industrial data.
